'''''Salix nigra''''', or the '''black willow''', is a species of [[willow]] native to a large portion of [[North America]], from [[New Brunswick]] and southern [[Ontario]] west to [[Arizona]] and [[California]], and south to northern [[Florida]] and [[Texas]].<ref name="grin">{{GRIN|id=102718|name=Salix nigra}}</ref>

== Description ==
[[File:Salix nigra catkins 8001.JPG|thumb|left|Flowers]]
''Salix nigra'' is a medium-sized [[deciduous]] [[tree]], the largest North American species of willow, growing to {{convert|10|-|30|m|ft|round=5|abbr=on}} tall, exceptionally up to {{convert|45|m|ft|abbr=on}}, with a trunk {{convert|50|–|80|cm|sigfig=1|sp=us}} diameter. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is dark brown to blackish, becoming fissured in older trees, and frequently forking near the base.<ref name="ReferenceA">Peattie, Donald Culross. Trees You Want to Know. Whitman Publishing Company, Racine, Wisconsin, 1934</ref> The shoots are slender and variable in color from green to brown, yellow or purplish; they are (like the related European ''[[Salix × fragilis|Salix fragilis]]'') brittle at the base, snapping evenly at the branch junction if bent sharply. The foliage buds are {{convert|2|–|4|mm|in|frac=16}} long, with a single, pointed reddish-brown bud scale. The [[leaf|leaves]] are alternate, long, thin, {{convert|5|–|15|cm|0|sp=us}} long and {{convert|0.5|–|2|cm|in|frac=8|sp=us}} broad, usually somewhat [[leaf shape|falcate]], dark, shiny green on both sides or with a lighter green underside, with a finely serrated margin, a short [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] and a pair of small [[stipule]]s. It is [[Plant sexuality|dioecious]], with small, greenish yellow to yellow [[flower]]s borne on [[catkin]]s {{convert|2.5|-|7.5|cm|in|frac=8|sp=us}} long in early spring at the same time as the new leaves appear. The [[fruit]] is a {{convert|5|mm|in|frac=16|sp=us}} [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]] which splits open when mature to release the numerous minute, down-covered [[seed]]s. The leaves turn a lemon yellow in the fall.<ref name="ReferenceA" />

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Salix nigra'' is native to a large portion of [[North America]], from [[New Brunswick]] and southern [[Ontario]] west to [[California]] and [[Arizona]], and south to northern [[Florida]] and [[Texas]].<ref name = "grin" /> It is also found in parts of Mexico, both south and west of the Rio Grande. It has also been introduced along streams in the state of Utah.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Salix nigra|url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/salnig/all.html|access-date=2020-11-29|website=www.fs.fed.us}}</ref> ''Salix nigra'' grows best in areas of full sun and wet or moist soils.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Salix nigra (Black Willow) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/salix-nigra/|access-date=2020-11-29|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref>  Thus, it is typically found along streams and in swamps.<ref>Tree Species of the World's Boreal Forests: http://www.borealforest.org/world/trees/black_willow.htm {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923193801/http://www.borealforest.org/world/trees/black_willow.htm |date=2015-09-23 }}</ref><ref>Trees of the North Carolina Piedmont: [http://www.ibiblio.org/openkey/intkey/web/SANI.htm ''Salix nigra'']</ref><ref>New Brunswick tree and shrub species of concern: [http://cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/subsite/mx-212/blackwillow ''Salix nigra''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071106044252/http://cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/subsite/mx-212/blackwillow|date=2007-11-06}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
Black willow is part of the [[Salicaceae]], the willow family.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=International Plant Names Index|url=https://www.ipni.org/|access-date=2020-11-18|website=www.ipni.org}}</ref> The accepted name for black willow is: ''Salix nigra'' Marshall. [[Humphry Marshall|Marshall]], the "Father of American [[Dendrology]]",<ref name=":0" /> first described this taxon in 1785. 

''[[Salix gooddingii]]'' (Goodding's willow) is sometimes considered a [[Variety (botany)|variety]] of ''S. nigra'' as ''S. nigra'' var. ''vallicola'' Dudley; when recognized, this extends the range of ''S. nigra'' to western North America. However, the two are usually treated as distinct species.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Plants Profile for Salix gooddingii (Goodding's willow)|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=SAGO|access-date=2020-11-18|website=plants.usda.gov}}</ref> Some other related taxa and synonyms are ''S. nigra'' var. ''altissima, S. nigra'' var. ''brevijulis, S. nigra'' var. ''longifolia, S. nigra'' var. ''marginata,'' and ''S. nigra'' var. ''wardii.''<ref>{{Cite web|title=SERNEC Collection Search Parameters|url=https://sernecportal.org/portal/collections/list.php|access-date=2020-11-18|website=sernecportal.org}}</ref>

Another name occasionally used for black willow is "swamp willow", not to be confused with ''[[Salix myrtilloides]]'' (swamp willow). Other common names include "Goodding willow", "southwestern black willow", "Dudley willow", and "sauz" (a [[Spanish language|Spanish]] word).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Black Willow - Salix nigra|url=https://www.cirrusimage.com/tree_black_willow/|access-date=2020-11-18|website=North American Insects & Spiders|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Reproduction and growth ==
''Salix nigra'' is [[Plant sexuality|dioecious]], which means it has separate male and female trees.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Dictionary by Merriam-Webster: America's most-trusted online dictionary|url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/|access-date=2020-11-29|website=www.merriam-webster.com|language=en}}</ref> Flowering may be climate dependent. It flowers during February in the southern part of its range, and flowers until June in the northern parts. These trees are capable of producing seeds when they are around the age of 10 years. The black willow continuously has good seed crops year after year, with only a few failures. The seeds require very specific conditions to germinate. They prefer soil that is very wet or flooded. After they germinate, they can experience excellent growth if they are exposed to high sunlight and copious moisture during the growing season.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Salix nigra Marsh|url=https://www.srs.fs.usda.gov/pubs/misc/ag_654/volume_2/salix/nigra.htm|access-date=2020-11-29|website=www.srs.fs.usda.gov}}</ref>

Black willow are capable of developing special features related to flood tolerance to help them survive in flooded habitats.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pezeshki |first=S. Reza |last2=Anderson |first2=Peter H. |last3=Shields |first3=F. Douglas |date=1998 |title=Effects of soil moisture regimes on growth and survival of black willow (Salix nigra) posts (cuttings) |url=https://www.infona.pl/resource/bwmeta1.element.springer-f6646cc7-7465-3962-8fe2-caac88e896bb |journal=Wetlands |language=English |volume=3 |issue=18 |pages=460–470 |doi=10.1007/BF03161538 |issn=0277-5212|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Under flooded conditions, black willow develop hypertrophied [[lenticels]] and water roots. Black willows are also sensitive to drought conditions. Black willows living in drought conditions experience inhibition of their branch and root growth.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pezeshki|first1=S. Reza|last2=Anderson|first2=Peter H.|last3=Shields|first3=F. Douglas|date=September 1998|title=Effects of soil moisture regimes on growth and survival of black willow (Salix nigra) posts (cuttings)|journal=Wetlands|volume=18|issue=3|pages=460–470|doi=10.1007/bf03161538|s2cid=23904993|issn=0277-5212}}</ref>

Early season leaves of some species in the ''Salix'' genus generally contain denser [[indumentum]] than leaves that are produced later in the season. Indumentum refers to hairs that are red or brown in color. ''Salix'' have first leaves, which are leaves that grow from the bud, and can also be called leaves that are "preformed".  The leaves that form as the branch continues to grow out are called new leaves, or "neoformed".<ref>{{Cite web|title=Salix: Dichotomous Key: Go Botany|url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/dkey/salix/|access-date=2020-11-29|website=gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org}}</ref>

== Largest example ==
According to the [[National Register of Champion Trees]], the largest black willow tree in the US is in [[Washington County, Minnesota]]. As of its last measurement in 2017, its height is {{convert|91|ft}}, circumference is {{convert|315|in}} and crown spread is {{convert|75|ft}}.<ref>[https://nationalchampiontree.org/championTree/6167/ Salix nigra Tree ID 6167]</ref>

The Marlboro Tree, located in [[Marlboro Township, New Jersey]] is certified by the [[New Jersey|State of New Jersey]] as the largest known example of this tree in the state. It is about 152 years old and measures {{convert|76|ft}} in height and {{convert|19.7|ft}} in circumference. Five grown people must hold hands to fully encircle the tree.<ref>[http://lcweb2.loc.gov/diglib/legacies/NJ/200003335.html Marlboro Tree]</ref>

== Uses ==
Black willow roots are very bitter and have been used as a substitute for [[quinine]] in the past.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Gunn|first1=John C.|title=Gunn's Newest Family Physician|location=Google Books|pages=807–811|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8OYrAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA809 |access-date=2014-12-23|year=1883}}</ref> Ethnobotanical uses of black willow by various Native American tribes include basketry, and treatment of fever, headache, and coughs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://herb.umd.umich.edu/herb/search.pl?searchstring=Salix+nigra|title = BRIT - Native American Ethnobotany Database}}</ref>

The black willow is the only willow native to the United States to be used as timber for a variety of different items. Black willow lumber is used in furniture and shipping containers. The largest production site for black willow timber was in Louisiana at its peak during the 1970s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fpl.fs.fed.us/documnts/usda/amwood/271black.pdf|title=Black Willow, An American Wood|date=July 1985|website=United States Department of Agriculture}}</ref>

The wood of ''Salix nigra'' is very lightweight. The wood was once used for [[Prosthesis|artificial limbs]], such as wooden hands.<ref name="Black Willow - Salix nigra">{{Cite web|title=Black Willow - Salix nigra|url=https://www.cirrusimage.com/tree_black_willow/|access-date=2020-11-29|website=North American Insects & Spiders|language=en-US}}</ref> It is also capable of maintaining its shape, does not splinter very easily, and has a moderately high shock resistance, allowing it to sustain continuous moderate impacts.<ref name="Black Willow - Salix nigra"/>

It is also used in environmental restoration, especially as an [[erosion control]] tool. Black willow is very resistant to herbivory and flooding. ''Salix nigra'' is used for marshland stabilization or restoration projects as long as the roots don't penetrate any clay liner that may be in place.<ref>S. Li, L. Martin, S. Pezeshki and F. Shields, "Responses of black willow (Salix nigra) cuttings to simulated herbivory and flooding", Acta Oecologica, vol. 28, no. 2, pp. 173–180, 2005.</ref><ref>Clemson University, "Salix nigra Marsh", /www.clemson.edu, 2016. [Online]. Available:http://www.na.fs.fed.us/spfo/pubs/silvics_manual/volume_2/salix/nigra.htm.[Accessed: 10- Jun- 2016].</ref> ''Salix nigra'' demonstrated some success as a photodegradation tool.<ref name="R. Conger 2003">R. Conger, Black willow (Salix nigra) use in phytoremediation techniques to remove the herbicide bentazon from shallow groundwater. [Baton Rouge, La.]: [Louisiana State University], 2003.</ref> [[Photodegradation]] is theorized to work by drawing the target chemical, such as [[bentazon]], up the roots and stem into the leaves where it is degraded by high-energy radiation provided by the sun.<ref name="R. Conger 2003"/>

== Disease ==
Black willows are susceptible to diseases such as [[crown gall]] and [[canker]]s. Crown gall is caused by bacteria living in the soil where the black willow is present. When black willow are infected, the [[bacteria]] stimulate a quick burst in growth of plant cells. They cause the tree to form tumor-like growths, or "galls" on different parts of the tree such as their roots or on the lower branches. As these galls get bigger, they become hard, woody, brown in color, and corky. Black willows do not normally die from crown galls. However, these galls can cause a disruption in the flow of nutrients throughout the tree and can have its normal growth stunted or slowed down due to this disease. Crown galls are less problematic in soils that are more acidic; thus, [[soil pH]] can be an important factor in helping to limit this disease.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Crown Galls|url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/gardens-gardening/your-garden/help-for-the-home-gardener/advice-tips-resources/pests-and-problems/diseases/bacterial-galls/crown-galls.aspx|access-date=2020-11-29|website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref>

Black canker disease is caused by the [[fungus]] ''[[Glomerella miyabeana]]''. This disease starts as spotting on the leaves of the black willow, where it then spreads to the petiole and eventually the twig or branch holding the leaf. It then forms black patches on the stem of the tree that are capable of expanding. Black willows that are in nutrient-poor locations or that are experiencing poor temporary climate conditions (such as a temporary lack of rainfall or short, [[drought]]-like conditions) are considered stressed and very susceptible to the spread of these cankers. Tissue on the black willow that is affected by these cankers will not grow with the rest of the tree, and cracks will begin to form.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Black Canker of Willow|url=https://www.purduelandscapereport.org/article/black-canker-of-willow/|access-date=2020-11-29|website=Purdue Landscape Report|language=en-US}}</ref>
